text.p: Sterling held on to the bulk of this week's sharp gains on Friday, climbing to its highest level against the mark since August 1991 due to expectations of further British interest rate increases.

The pound has now cleared its old central parity in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at 2.95 marks, a target which proved unsustainable during Britain's abortive membership of the system between 1990 and 1992.
Traders said on Friday, however, that there was little to stop sterling rising to three marks and beyond in the weeks ahead.

"Everyone and his mother and brother wants to buy sterling at the moment. Even on a quiet day like today there was still demand out of the U.S.," said Peter Wood, currency trader at Bank of Boston in London.
Most U.S. markets were shut for the July 4 Independence Day holiday.

Analysts said brisk demand for the pound was likely to persist before a meeting of the Bank of England's policy-making council next Wednesday and Thursday due to expectations of a rise in base lending rates of as much as half a percentage point.
At 1500 GMT the pound was trading at 2.9620/30 marks compared with 2.9580/90 in late European trade on Thursday and just below a 70-month high of 2.9650 set earlier in the afternoon.
Against the dollar, sterling was at $1.6874/81 compared with $1.6900/10 late on Thursday and shy of a five month high at $1.6920 set on Thursday.
The broadest measure of sterling strength, its index against a trade-weighted basket of global currencies, set a six-year high at 103.9 in late trade.

"The market has built an aggressive UK interest rate forecast post-budget and the other side of the equation in Germany is still truly awful," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank. "In that situation, you can't rule out sterling at three marks."
Traders said there was still no sign of Bank of England intervention on the currency markets to cap sterling.
Investors and speculators searching for attractive interest rate returns in a low yield global environment are flocking to the pound, analysts said.

Fuelled by robust economic growth, Britain has the highest base lending rates of the major world economies at 6.5 percent. Only Ireland at 6.75 percent and Greece with a discount rate at 14.50 percent are higher in the European Union.
The British interest rate market is now discounting at least a half-point rise in interest rates by September.

"Sterling looks technically stretched today but there is nothing to stop it going back up and testing 3.0 (marks)," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC Markets. "The UK is the only country that requires sustained rate rises."

Wednesday's 1997/98 budget from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown triggered sterling's latest surge as the fiscal tightening was seen as insufficient to rein in strong consumer demand. This leaves interest rates to take up the slack, economists said.

Interest rates are expected to remain low in continental Europe as a result of sluggish economic activity, high unemployment and tight fiscal policies aimed at meeting guidelines for European monetary union.

Even in the United States, the market is scaling back expectations of higher interest rates. The June U.S. employment report on Thursday again showed no sign of inflationary pressures in the economy despite brisk economic growth.
